title: Conflict, aggression and lone working
siteNotes: Who to call first for help on each shift (duty manager) and their numbers
The lone-working check-in procedure: who you tell, how often and what happens if you miss a check-in
Which areas are remote or risky when working alone (cellar, car park, outbuildings, marquee) and the plan for each
Where incidents of aggression and abuse are reported and recorded
Late closing routine: who locks up, who leaves with whom, how staff get home safely
legalNotes: Employers must assess risks to staff, including violence and lone working, and protect them: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999. Duty on the employer from HSE guidance (hse.gov.uk/lone-working).

HSE guidance on lone workers (hse.gov.uk/lone-working/worker): employees must take care of their own health and safety and that of others, cooperate with the employer, and talk to a manager or supervisor if worried. Verified. HSE leaflet: Protecting lone workers (INDG73).
HSE says employers should train, supervise and monitor lone workers, keep in touch, and respond to incidents. This was taken from a search summary of the HSE page and not read in full: flagged.

De-escalation steps (calm voice, space, listening, not arguing), warning signs and the 'safe distance and exit' approach are good practice. Not tied to a statute and not verified against one HSE page: flagged.

The session says violence and abuse of staff is not part of the job. This is the HSE position on work-related violence and the employer's duty to manage the risk. The HSE violence toolkit page could not be retrieved: flagged.
Self-defence and use of force: not taught. The session says to withdraw and call for help. Any legal detail on reasonable force is not covered and was not verified.
Not verified: whether the venue has a lone-working policy in writing. Treated as a site matter.

Review 6 Oct 2026: the legal duty is to assess the risk and put reasonable control measures in place (Management Regs 1999 reg. 3; HSWA 1974 s.2). HSE lone-working guidance says lone working is not itself prohibited and that employers should consider monitoring and keeping in touch; that is guidance on how to manage the risk, not a rule that employers must check in with each worker. Three sentences were reworded accordingly. The definition of a lone worker (no close or direct supervision) is HSE's. Employees' own duties (take reasonable care, co-operate, report) come from HSWA s.7 and Management Regs reg. 14.

cards.kicker: Front of house, bar, housekeeping and events · 12 minutes
cards.title: Conflict, aggression and lone working
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- keep calm and de-escalate an angry guest
- know when to step back and get help
- stay safe when you work alone or late

cards.title: Abuse is not part of the job
cards.body:
Shouting, threats and violence from guests are not something you have to put up with. Your employer must assess the risk and take reasonable steps to protect you, including when you work alone.

Your part is to look after yourself and others, and to report what happens.

items.title: Your part
items.text: Take care and follow the plan

cards.title: Calm it down
cards.body:
Most anger comes from a problem the guest wants solved: a cold meal, a wait, a bill. Take it seriously. Keep your voice low and slow. Do not argue, even if they are wrong.

> People calm down when they feel heard.

items.title: Space
items.text: Stand to the side, an arm's length or more

items.title: Listen
items.text: Let them finish; nod, do not interrupt

items.title: Solve or pass on
items.text: Offer what you can; fetch a manager

cards.title: When it is getting worse
cards.body: Watch for changes. Act early, before it turns physical. If more than one of these appears, step back and get help.

cards.title: Distance and a way out
cards.body:
Keep a safe distance and know where your exit is. Do not let a guest stand between you and the door. Do not turn your back, and do not block them in.

You are never expected to put yourself at risk to win an argument.

left.title: Do
items: Call 999 if anyone is in danger

cards.title: Who to get and when
cards.body:
Tell a manager when a guest is abusive, not accepting an answer, or you feel unsafe. Your manager will show you who to call. Call 999 if someone is being hurt or threatened with violence.

Afterwards, report it, however small it felt. Write down what happened.

items.title: Call a colleague
items.text: Two people are safer than one

cards.title: Lone working and late closing
cards.body:
A lone worker is anyone without close or direct supervision. Your employer must assess the risks of working alone and put sensible arrangements in place, such as keeping in touch and responding if something happens.

Your manager will show you the check-in procedure. Do not enter a remote area such as the cellar without a plan.

✔ Tell someone where you are
✔ Keep your phone with you
✘ Do not leave alone at night if you are worried

items.title: Say where
items.text: Tell someone where you are working

cards.title: Report it, every time
cards.body:
Report threats, abuse and near misses to your manager, even if you handled it. Reports help us spot patterns and change how we work.

If you are shaken, say so. Support is part of the response.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Abuse and violence are not part of the job.
- Stay calm, keep your distance and listen.
- Know your exit. Step back and get help early.
- Check in when you work alone, and plan before going to remote areas.
- Report everything.

cards.q: A guest is shouting about a long wait for his meal. What is your first move?
options: Tell him to calm down
Listen and acknowledge his frustration
Explain that the kitchen is short-staffed
Walk away without a word
cards.why: Listening and acknowledging calms most people. Telling someone to calm down or arguing usually makes it worse.

cards.q: If a guest threatens you, you should stand your ground until the guest backs down.
cards.why: Keep a safe distance, withdraw and get help. You do not have to stay in a threatening situation.

cards.q: You are closing the bar on your own late at night and need to change a barrel in the cellar. What should happen first?
options: Go straight down, it is only a minute
Tell someone where you are going
Prop the door open and go down
Leave it and tell nobody at all
cards.why: Never go to a remote area alone without a plan. Tell someone where you are and follow the venue's check-in procedure.

cards.q: Which TWO are warning signs that a situation is getting more dangerous?
options: A guest sighing at a wait
A guest standing very close and shouting
A guest asking for the manager
A guest blocking your way or clenching fists
A guest asking for the Wi-Fi code
cards.why: Invading your space, shouting, blocking you or clenched fists show escalation. Step back and get help.

cards.q: Reporting a minor incident of abuse is worthwhile, even if you handled it yourself.
cards.why: Reports show patterns and let managers act before something worse happens.

cards.q: A guest is shouting at you across the counter. Where should you stand?
options: Right in front, to show you are not afraid
Behind the guest, so you can watch them
Side-on, exit clear, arm's length or more
Leaning right against the door, blocking it
cards.why: A safe distance and a clear way out protect you. Do not let a guest stand between you and the door.

cards.q: You should stay with an angry guest until they calm down, even if they threaten you.
cards.why: If you feel threatened, withdraw and get help. You are never expected to put yourself at risk.

cards.q: Which of these is a warning sign that you should call 999?
options: The guest is pushing a colleague and threatening them
The guest is complaining loudly about the bill
The guest keeps asking to see the manager
The guest swears under their breath at you
cards.why: Violence or a threat of violence to someone needs the emergency services.

cards.q: You are closing alone and feel uneasy about walking to the car park. What do you do?
options: Go, since it is only a minute away
Leave the lights on and hope for the best
Wait until someone happens to arrive
Tell your manager; follow the late routine
cards.why: Say so. Your manager will show you the late-closing routine, and your employer must put sensible protection in place for lone workers.

cards.q: Abuse from guests is simply part of working in hospitality and need not be reported.
cards.why: Abuse and violence are not part of the job. Report it so patterns can be seen and action taken.
